content: 1. The 2012 guidelines for response progress reporting were developed to construct core indicators for monitoring the implementation of the 2011 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS. These guidelines were published by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) in Geneva in 2011. 2. The 2014 global AIDS response progress reporting guidelines were created to establish core indicators for tracking the progress of the 2011 United Nations Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS. These were also published by UNAIDS in Geneva in 2014. 3. Vickerman et al. conducted model projections to determine the required coverage of syringe distribution programs necessary to prevent HIV epidemics among people who inject drugs. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (JAIDS) in 2006, volume 42, issue 3, pages 355–361. 4. Heimer explored community coverage and HIV prevention by assessing metrics for estimating HIV incidence through syringe exchange programs. This study was published in the International Journal on Drug Policy in 2008, supplement 1, pages S65–S73. 5. A supplementary tool to the 2014 Consolidated Guidelines for HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations was developed to assist in setting and monitoring targets. 6. Des Jarlais and Friedman reviewed 15 years of research on preventing HIV infection among people who inject drugs. They discussed what has been learned, what remains unknown, what actions have been taken, and what gaps persist. This review was published in Public Health Reports in 1998, supplement 1, pages 182–188. 7. Bobashev and Zule modeled the impact of high dead-space syringes on the HIV epidemic among people who inject drugs. Their study was published in Addiction in 2010, volume 105, issue 8, pages 1439–1447. 8. Zule and Bobashev examined the association between high dead-space syringes and the risk of HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections among people who inject drugs. Their findings were published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence in 2009, volume 100, issue 3, pages 204–213. 9. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a guide in 2011 for monitoring and evaluating national HIV testing and counseling (HTC) programs. This was a field-test version designed to improve program effectiveness. 10. WHO also released a handbook in 2010 aimed at improving HIV testing and counseling services. This field-test version provided practical guidance for service enhancement. 11. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), UNAIDS, and WHO jointly published guidelines in 2009 on HIV testing and counseling in prisons and other closed settings. This document was released in Vienna. 12. UNAIDS outlined ambitious treatment targets in 2014, aiming to write the final chapter of the AIDS epidemic. This publication emphasized the importance of achieving these goals to end the epidemic. 13. WHO issued consolidated guidelines in 2013 on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection. These guidelines provided comprehensive recommendations for clinical and public health practices. 14. The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria developed a monitoring and evaluation toolkit in 2011. Part 5 of this toolkit focused on strengthening health and community systems to improve outcomes in HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria programs. 15. Stangl, Brady, and Fritz authored a technical brief in 2012 on measuring HIV-related stigma and discrimination. This document was published by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and the International Centre for Research on Women. It provided methodologies for assessing stigma and its impact on HIV outcomes.
